Source (default): Exclusion terms loaded from notes/agencies_to_be_excluded.txt Override (keep list present): If notes/nuclear_waste_projects_to_keep.csv exists, then all Nuclear + Waste Management projects are excluded except those in the keep list, which were determined by CAFT to be project relevant.
Rationale: Nuclear waste cleanup, storage, and legacy site management are not clean energy production.
Note: The keep list represents client-reviewed exceptions and is authoritative when present. This switches the filter to a tag-based rule for Nuclear + Waste, reclassifying all others to “Other.” Clean energy count reduced by ~1,554 (from ~22,279 to ~20,725).





Location: Same as Filter 3, extended to check project_title Applies: Only when the keep list is not present (default mode)
Criteria: Same as Filter 3, but also checks project_title field for exclusion terms.
Rationale: Some projects had missing or incomplete project_sponsor fields, causing them to slip through the original filter. For example, “Hanford Site” might appear only in the title. This catches such cases.
Impact: Captured ~84 additional projects that were previously misclassified.

title: NEPA
text:
Refactor Architecture
Add a ProcessConfig object and make pipeline behavior config-driven. Fields: process_type, doc_priority, doc_include, doc_exclude, cue_patterns, guardrails, final_date_rules, confidence_rules. Create three configs: CE_CONFIG, EA_CONFIG, EIS_CONFIG. Keep one shared execution flow; switch behavior by config only. Split extract_timeline.py into logical modules (can stay in one file initially, then move). timeline_config.py: process configs and cue libraries. timeline_documents.py: doc filtering and section-level inclusion/exclusion. timeline_candidates.py: regex date extraction + context windows. timeline_classifier.py: BERT inference wrapper + label mapping. timeline_rules.py: guardrails and post-classification normalization. timeline_finalize.py: exactly-two-date resolver. timeline_runner.py: orchestration and CLI entrypoints. Add a clear orchestrator API. run_timeline(process_types=[“CE”], energy_type=“Clean”, sample_size=None, output_file=None) Loop per process_type, load config, run same stages, append outputs. Persist one row per project with required outputs: initiation_date_final decision_date_final initiation_confidence decision_confidence initiation_provenance decision_provenance process_type timeline_status (complete, missing_initiation, missing_decision, ambiguous) Parameterization by Process Type
Document policy by process. CE: current approach remains. EA: prioritize FONSI, Decision Notice/Memo, final EA, then draft EA. EIS: prioritize ROD, final EIS, NOI/scoping notices, then draft EIS. Cue library by process. Shared labels stay: initiation, review, decision, other, plus optional expiration, historical. CE cues stay mostly unchanged. EA cues add stronger FONSI/EA-specific terms. EIS cues add stronger NOI/ROD/NOA/publication language. Final-date rules by process. CE: current signature-centric decision logic. EA: prefer FONSI/Decision Notice date over general signatures. EIS: prefer ROD date over FEIS publication date; initiation prefers NOI/scoping publication. Run Strategy Recommendation
Implement and validate EA first, then EIS (separate passes). Reason: easier debugging, clearer error attribution, smaller domain shift per pass. EA and EIS have different dominant decision artifacts (FONSI vs ROD). After both are stable, run EA+EIS together using per-process configs. Keep separate metrics by process in the same run. Do not mix CE in early stabilization runs. Bring CE back only after EA/EIS error rates converge. Final production mode: process_types=[“CE”,“EA”,“EIS”] with per-type configs and per-type evaluation report. EA/EIS Document Filtering
Prioritize these document types. EA decision: FONSI, Decision Notice, Decision Memo, signed approval pages. EIS decision: ROD. Initiation: NOI, scoping notices, early notice/publication docs. Secondary: final EA/FEIS if no explicit decision doc date exists. Exclude or de-prioritize. Appendices, technical appendices, references/bibliography-heavy sections, maps/figures tables of data. Generic cover pages unless they contain explicit decision/initiation cues. Boilerplate form metadata not tied to project action milestones. Section-level heuristics. Upweight pages containing headers like Record of Decision, Finding of No Significant Impact, Notice of Intent, Decision Notice. Downweight pages with citation-heavy patterns and form-template boilerplate. Cue Library Additions for EA/EIS
Initiation cues to add. notice of intent, noi, published in the federal register, scoping period, scoping meeting, notice of availability (for early stage context). Decision cues to add. EA: finding of no significant impact, fonsi, decision notice, decision memorandum. EIS: record of decision, rod signed, selected alternative, agency decision. Review/intermediate cues to keep distinct. draft eis, draft ea, public comment, comment period, final eis filed, response to comments. Keep these from being promoted to decision unless strong decision cues are present. Exactly-Two-Date Normalization Rules
Candidate ranking. Build scored candidate lists separately for initiation and decision. Score components: cue strength, doc-type priority, signer-title strength, context quality, temporal plausibility. Initiation resolution. Prefer earliest strong initiation from NOI/scoping/application cues. If missing, allow explicit fallback to earliest strong review with initiation_imputed=True. Decision resolution. Prefer strongest doc-specific decision cue (ROD/FONSI/Decision Notice) over generic signatures. Use latest only among high-strength decision candidates, not across all candidates. Confidence and provenance. Confidence tiers: high, medium, low from score thresholds. Provenance payload should include: doc_type, document_id, page_number, matched_text, cue_type, rule_path. Modeling Strategy (EA/EIS sample size constraints)
Risks. Overfitting due to small labeled EA/EIS sets. Class imbalance (initiation typically sparse). Domain shift from CE wording and structure. Recommended training approach. Phase 1: train a shared base classifier on CE+EA+EIS with strict balanced sampling across process and label. Phase 2: process-specific calibration layer via rules and thresholds per config. Optional Phase 3: light fine-tuning heads for EA and EIS only if shared model underperforms. Prevent CE domination. Per-batch stratified sampling by process_type and label. Class weights for initiation. Cap CE examples per epoch to near EA+EIS combined count. Validate by process-specific metrics, not only aggregate metrics. Evaluation Plan
Build a gold set. EA: 100-150 projects. EIS: 100-150 projects. Double-annotate a subset for agreement. Metrics. Date-level precision/recall for initiation and decision separately. Exact-match and tolerance-window match (±7 and ±30 days). Completion rate for exactly-two-date outputs. Temporal sanity checks: initiation <= decision, and duration distribution review. Error analysis loop. Slice errors by process, doc type, agency, cue path, and fallback mode. Track top failure patterns and map each to either cue updates or guardrail updates. Promotion gates. Do not merge EA/EIS into all-process run until each process clears target thresholds on gold set and sanity checks. No repository changes were made.

title: Project Overview

This document is a good reference for how to contextualize this project, the project goals and data, and to clearly understand the project deliverables and timeline.


Federal environmental permitting—and, relatedly, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)—has often been blamed as a core contributor to delays in infrastructure deployment. However, research to date on NEPA has been hindered by federal agency data management practices: NEPA documents are scattered across numerous agency databases, often in machine-unreadable formats, and typically lack basic metadata and other identifiers. As such, researchers have had to craft bespoke subsets of NEPA data from which to glean insights—a time-consuming task that has limited the information available about NEPA’s effectiveness and paved the way for a national permitting reform conversation rife with anecdotes and cherry-picked information.
The newly released National Environmental Policy Act Text Corpus (NEPATEC) 2.0 dataset from the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory’s (PNNL’s) PermitAI project has the potential to add new, more comprehensive evidence into this conversation. PNNL has built and released a comprehensive dataset of past environmental reviews and permitting documents containing millions of pages and billions of words in machine-readable JSON format. The database contains more than 120,000 NEPA documents1 (categorical exclusions, draft and final environmental assessments, draft and final environmental impact statements, records of decision, findings of no significant impact, and other supporting documentation) from 60,000 projects prepared by more than 60 different agencies. Each document contains metadata for (as applicable):
• Lead agency
• Category
• Type of review
• Name of project
• Location
• Project sponsor
• Project sector
• Project type (a subset of project sector)
• Type of document
• Document title
• Agency or contractor responsible for preparing the document
• Categorical exclusion category 
• Summary of the proposed action
The National Environmental Policy Act Text Corpus (NEPATEC) 2.0 can be accessed here on huggingface.

Data on number of clean energy projects within the dataset: number of projects broken down by technology (e.g., offshore and onshore wind, solar, geothermal, nuclear), lead agency, and location

Broken out by number of projects, generation capacity, and change over time

Are the Post-FRA sample sizes large enough to draw meaningful conclusions?

Executive Summary






Key Findings




Document length has declined Post-FRA, but remains well above statutory limits. Mean EA page counts fell ~22% (142 to 111 pages) and mean EIS page counts fell ~25% (535 to 403 pages) after FRA enactment.
Compliance with FRA page limits is low. Only 42% of Post-FRA EAs meet the 75-page limit, and just 12% of Post-FRA EISs meet the 150-page standard limit. The majority of EIS projects (69%) exceed even the 300-page extraordinary complexity threshold.
Post-FRA sample sizes are small (33 EAs, 42 EISs), limiting the strength of conclusions. The analysis covers 627 clean energy projects total (552 Pre-FRA, 75 Post-FRA).
Trends were already declining before FRA. The rolling average and LOESS trend lines suggest document length was decreasing prior to June 2023, meaning the observed post-FRA decline may partially reflect pre-existing trends rather than FRA-driven compliance.



This analysis examines whether document length has changed after FRA enactment, using clean energy EA and EIS projects with final documents and complete timelines. This report delivers the following:

Data on the number of pages over time, including pre- and post-Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (FRA), which set page limit requirements.

The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (Public Law 118-5) introduced page limits for NEPA environmental reviews as part of broader permitting reform. Environmental Assessments (EAs) are limited to 75 pages, while Environmental Impact Statements (EISs) are limited to 150 pages, with an exception of up to 300 pages for extraordinarily complex projects. This analysis examines document length trends for clean energy EA and EIS projects to assess whether these page limits have had an observable effect.

title: NEPA Clean Energy Analysis: Deliverable 5
text:
Scope and Inclusion Criteria
This analysis is restricted to:

Process types: Environmental Assessments (EA) and Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) only. Categorical Exclusions (CE) are excluded because FRA page limits do not apply to CEs.
Document types: Final Environmental Assessments and Final Environmental Impact Statements (FEIS) only. Draft documents are excluded.
Timeline requirement: Only projects with both non-missing initiation and decision dates (from LLM-adjudicated timeline data) are included.
Clean energy: Only projects classified as clean energy in the NEPATEC 2.0 database.

When multiple final documents exist for a single project, the document flagged as main_document = TRUE is preferred; ties are broken by highest page count.






FRA Classification Rule



Projects are classified as Post-FRA when their decision date is on or after June 3, 2023. Even if a project was initiated before the FRA, it is expected to comply with the page limits if its final decision came after enactment. This reflects the forward-looking nature of the statute.

Rolling Average
Figure 2 shows the 6-month rolling average of document page counts over time for EA and EIS projects, from 2010 to the present. The red dashed line marks the FRA enactment date (June 3, 2023). Monthly raw averages are omitted because small sample sizes in individual months introduce noise; the rolling average smooths this to reveal underlying trends.





Figure 2: 6-month rolling average of mean monthly page counts for clean energy EA and EIS projects (2010–2025). The red dashed line marks FRA enactment on June 3, 2023.

Project-Level Scatter
Figure 3 plots each individual project by its decision date and total pages, with a LOESS trend line and 95% confidence interval. This view complements the rolling average by showing the full dispersion of project-level data and highlighting any shifts in the distribution after FRA enactment.





Figure 3: Individual project page counts by decision date (2010–2025). Each point represents one project; the blue curve is a LOESS trend with 95% confidence interval. The red dashed line marks FRA enactment.

Average and Median Page Counts
Figure 4 compares mean and median document length for projects decided before and after FRA enactment. Bar height represents the mean page count, while the diamond marker indicates the median. Sample sizes are displayed on each bar.





Figure 4: Mean total pages for clean energy EA and EIS projects, Pre- vs Post-FRA. Bar height = mean; diamond = median. Projects are classified by decision date relative to June 3, 2023.

Distribution Comparison
Figure 5 shows the full distribution of page counts before and after FRA using violin plots (showing distribution shape) overlaid with box plots (showing quartiles and outliers). This reveals whether observed changes in the mean are driven by a general shift in the distribution or by movement in the tails.





Figure 5: Distribution of document page counts, Pre- vs Post-FRA. Violin plots show distribution shape; box plots show quartiles. Diamond markers indicate median values. Y-axis capped at the 99th percentile to improve readability.
